summary: This file provides utilities for integrating Bluesky social media engagement into a Docusaurus blog. It defines TypeScript interfaces for Bluesky API responses and blog metadata, exports functions to fetch blocked user lists and engagement metrics (likes, reposts, replies), and provides React hooks that resolve which Bluesky post corresponds to a blog article and fetch engagement statistics for display.

explanations.5: This constant limits how many users we fetch per API call when getting likers or reposters, since the Bluesky API has pagination limits.
explanations.7: TTL stands for 'time-to-live' — this sets how long (5 minutes) we keep feed data cached in the browser's sessionStorage before fetching fresh data.
explanations.10: Similar to line 7, but for the blocked users list — we cache it for 1 hour since moderators don't add/remove people from lists frequently.
explanations.43: We use a Set here instead of an array because we might see the same person like AND repost a post, and we want to track all their actions without duplicates.
explanations.108: This recursively walks through a tree of replies to collect all the people who replied to the post, flattening the nested structure into a single list.
explanations.110: We define a nested function `walk` so we can call it recursively to traverse nested reply threads without passing authors around.
explanations.132: The `record` function is a helper that either creates a new entry for an actor or updates their existing one with a new engagement action (like, repost, or comment).
explanations.137: The logical OR chain checks the cache first — if this actor already exists in our map, use that entry; otherwise create a fresh one.
explanations.153: We sort by the number of actions in descending order so people who engaged in multiple ways (liked AND reposted) appear first, since that signals stronger engagement.
explanations.158: We remove query parameters and trailing slashes so different URLs pointing to the same article (like `example.com/post` vs `example.com/post/`) get treated as identical.
explanations.169: This function handles pagination automatically — the Bluesky API returns a cursor to fetch the next page, and we loop until there are no more pages.
explanations.174: We parse the stored JSON and extract the timestamp so we can check if it's still fresh (not expired).
explanations.178: If the cached data is fresh enough (timestamp is within the TTL window), we return it immediately without making a network request.
explanations.188: URLSearchParams is a built-in way to construct query strings safely — it handles encoding special characters automatically.
explanations.195: The `??` operator provides a default empty array if `data.items` is undefined or null, so we safely iterate even if the API returns incomplete data.
explanations.213: This reads the feed cache from sessionStorage — returns the mapping of article URLs to their Bluesky record keys, or null if missing or expired.
explanations.261: This function builds a map by fetching the account owner's recent posts and extracting external links from them, so we can later match blog articles to Bluesky posts.
explanations.283: We drill into nested properties carefully — `embed?.external?.uri` uses optional chaining so we don't crash if any intermediate level is undefined.
explanations.287: We extract just the record key (last part of the URI path) and store it keyed by the normalized URL so we can quickly look it up later.
explanations.308: This hook tries multiple strategies to find the Bluesky record key: frontmatter override first, then look up in the author's post history, with fallback to source-language version.
explanations.322: Docusaurus's `permalink` already includes the locale's base URL, so we just append it to the site URL — we don't need to add baseUrl again.
explanations.325: For non-default locales, we strip off the locale's baseUrl prefix to get back to the slug, then reconstruct it as a source-locale URL.
explanations.329: We initialize state with the frontmatter key if provided, otherwise set `resolving: true` to indicate we need to fetch it.
explanations.345: We use a `cancelled` flag so if the component unmounts or dependencies change before the async fetch completes, we can ignore the stale result.
explanations.352: We try the current locale's URL first, then fall back to the source-language URL — this way translated articles see the English post's engagement unless they have their own.
explanations.382: We encode the URI in the query string to handle special characters safely, and request up to MAX_ACTORS_PER_ENDPOINT results per API call.
explanations.390: This ternary casts the response to the appropriate type (LikesResponse vs RepostedByResponse) based on which endpoint we called, then extracts the actor list.
explanations.404: This is the main hook that orchestrates everything — it fetches the post thread, blocked list, and then engagement metrics, returning stats for display components.
explanations.442: Promise.all runs both requests in parallel since neither depends on the other — the blocked list is cached anyway so it's usually instant.
explanations.445: If the blocked list fetch fails (network error, etc.), we catch and return an empty set so we can still show engagement, just without filtering.
explanations.448: We merge two sources of blocked handles: those hardcoded in the site config and those from the Bluesky moderation list.
explanations.469: The `resolvedUri` from the thread response uses the post's DID instead of the handle, which is required by getLikes and getRepostedBy APIs.
explanations.470: We only fetch likers if there's at least one like, and reposters if there's at least one repost — no point making an API call for zero results.
explanations.474: We use the setState callback form to merge the new likers/reposters into the existing engaged list, keeping the commenters we already fetched.
